resources.title: athefre: puzzle method development website
resources.author: Michael James Straughan (Athefre)
resources.level: intermediate to advanced (CMLL recognition and prediction, EOLR, DFDB, ACMLL, pseudo/non-matching blocks); much of the site is non-Roux method theory
resources.summary: A Google Site (HTTP 200, rendered with Playwright) by Michael James Straughan, a Roux user since 2006 who calls himself the first xy2-neutral Roux solver. The main page is a bio and a list of his developments. Credits he claims: EOLR and half of EOLRb (2012), DFDB recognition for 4c (2012), the NMCLL 2 pseudo-corner recognition (2010), ATCRM (2021, with Tim Mosher), Straughan minimum-sticker recognition (2024), ACMLL (2022), algorithm unions, NBRS group notation, LEG-1 (2x2), and cubinghistory.com. Navigation: 3x3 Methods (Nautilus, APB, Solaris, Polaris, Aetherman: not Roux), Roux (ACMLL, CMLL Prediction, OCLL Prediction, EOLR, DFDB Recognition, Iterative/Trigger CMLL), Steps & Concepts (13 pages), Recognition (11 pages), Other Puzzles, Writings, CubingHistory.com, plus Discord invites. I read the main page, all 6 Roux pages and 13 concept and recognition pages (12 bear on Roux; A2 is a 2x2 method). Roux content: (1) ACMLL. Build F2B imperfectly (flipped pair, outside pair, swapped pairs, front cycle, spiral) and let the CMLL alg fix the blocks. He claims 2-6 moves saved in SB, all-R/U pair inserts and deeper inspection. Stats: flipped pair FR 9.81 moves / 11.81 MCC and BR 9.67 / 12.35, against normal CMLL at 10.02 / 12.31. Outside DFr 9.63 / 13.11, DBr 10.05 / 12.47. Learning order: flipped FR/BR, then Outside, then Swap FL/FR, then Front Cycle. (2) CMLL Prediction. Compares recognition systems by sticker count: Straughan 4, ATCRM 5, U-sticker+pattern 6, Hyperorientations 6. Adds 'Intuitive CP', which tracks three L/R (or F/B) stickers during the last SB pair, reads the U-sticker positions as +/- (adjacent or diagonal) and names the swap. (3) OCLL Prediction. Orientation-sticker targeting during the last 2-3 moves of common last-pair inserts. Primary and secondary corners to watch. Facts such as 'UBR does not move during R U R', R U' R', R U2 R''. Prefer tracking-friendly last-pair solutions (M2 U M' r U r' rather than R U' R' U R U R'). (4) EOLR history. The 2012 'Misoriented Centers Table' held 285 hand-found solutions including mirrors and inverses. It is the first EOLR, plus about half of EOLRb. (5) DFDB. Track the DF+DB (or UF+UB) stickers during 4b and set the AUF for 4c from them. Credits Louis de Mendonca with popularising it. Links the FUBU/BUFU video by 'Michał Ciebiad' (as the page spells it) and cubinghistory 4c history. (6) Iterative/Trigger CMLL. A CMLL set built from a few triggers, generated with Batch Solver, for people who struggle with memorisation. ATCRM pages: first read the orientation of the L/R-coloured stickers (8 orientations with sub-orientations, 84 patterns for 42 algs), then two fixed stickers. One rule for R/R' non-matching blocks and transformation: on the right-side corners, treat U/D colours as non-U/D and the reverse. Pseudo depths N, P1 (NMB), P2 (transformation), P3. 'CxLL Recognition Systems' classifies 12 systems with inventor and year. 'Three Corner CxLL' (Jan 2026) recognises CMLL from the visible stickers of UFL, UFR and UBR only. 'Intuitive Corner Recognition' uses side-sticker colour order. NBRS notation: dL is the Roux left block, dLR is F2B, dFR is a pair. L7E extends LSE to 7 edges; SL5C and Transformation are side topics. Straughan Recognition is covered in depth by deep-web-7, and ACMLL and CMLL Prediction (with their sheets) by deep-web-3.
drills: ATCRM CMLL recognition: find the orientation of the four L/R-coloured stickers, then check two pre-set stickers. Add R/R' non-matching blocks and apply the right-side U/D flip rule
Straughan four-sticker CMLL tracking: follow FLU, FUR, RFU and RUB through the final SB pair and call the case before the insert finishes
Three-corner CMLL recognition using only the visible stickers of UFL, UFR and UBR (never UBL)
OCLL prediction: watch the two primary corners during the last 2-3 moves of the final pair insert, predict the CO case, then confirm with the secondary corner
Intuitive CP prediction: during the last pair find three L/R (or F/B) stickers, compare two opposite colours' U-sticker positions (+/-), and name the corner swap (left, right, front, back, diagonal)
ACMLL: insert the last SB pair flipped (FR/BR) or outside (DFr/DBr) with R/U moves only and finish with the matching ACMLL alg. Follow the suggested learning order
DFDB: during 4b track the DF/DB (or UF/UB) stickers and set the 4c AUF from them without pausing
Choose tracking-friendly last-pair solutions that leave the corners still until the final insert
Iterative/Trigger CMLL for learners: execute each CMLL as a chain of known triggers
infoTopics: Taxonomy of CMLL/CxLL recognition systems, with inventor and year: Waterman, Intuitive, 1-Side Sune, NMCxLL 2, ATCRM, Straughan positional, Straughan+ATCRM hybrid, NMCxLL, Hyperorientations, Permute First, Straughan object
Sticker counts per recognition system (4 / 5 / 6 / 6) and why fewer stickers help prediction
Pseudo depths: normal, P1 non-matching blocks, P2 transformation, P3 and beyond, and why L/R stickers keep their symmetry under L/R turns
ACMLL concept, benefits and movecount/MCC data
OCLL prediction mechanics for common final-pair inserts
EOLR/EOLRb origin (2012) and misoriented centres as a pseudo technique
DFDB origin, and its UF/UB variant
Group-reference notation (NBRS): dL, dR, dLR = F2B, dFR = pair, MES = core
xy2 colour neutrality for non-matching blocks
Transformation/conjugation (also used by 42), SL5C, L7E (an LSE extension for free-M-slice methods)

resources.title: reco.nz: reconstruction database (Roux filter)
resources.author: reco.nz team (Angus, Chunky Girl, Boots, Monke); reconstructions by community members such as Stewy, kyh, eff, rebuc, Brest, Louis de Mendonca
resources.level: all levels can study it; the data is mostly world-class 3x3 and OH Roux solves
resources.summary: A server-rendered reconstruction database (HTTP 200; rendered with Playwright and paged with curl). Important: the query parameter is case-sensitive. 'Roux=on' filters to Roux, but the lower-cased 'roux=on' in the key is ignored and lists every method (the first rows are CFOP and ZB). Counts with Roux=on, 50 rows per page: 1,186 Roux solves in total, 527 3x3 and 659 OH, and none for 4x4 or 5x5. Filters: sort by id, result, movecount or TPS (ascending or descending); Official/Unofficial; puzzle (3x3, 4x4-7x7, OH, SQ1); method (CFOP, Roux, ZB, ZZ, Petrus, Yau, Redux, Lin, Vandenbergh); solver multi-select; tags (WR, NAR, SAR, ER, AsR, OcR, AfR, NR, +2, DNF); and CFOP-only filters. List columns: ID, Puzzle, Result, Solver, Method, Date, Competition, Tags, Movecount, TPS, Reconstructed By. The newest Roux entries (Jul-Aug 2026) are Crimson Arradaza's OH world-record average of 7.72 at GAN Tarlac Speedcubing Open 2026, including a 6.82 single, and an NR average at Makati Heroes. The lowest 3x3 Roux movecounts are 27 STM (Zhouheng Sun 4.59, Fahmi Aulia Rachman 2.81) and 30 (Alexander Lau). A solve page shows the scramble and a step-commented solution: inspection, FB, SS (second square), SP (second pair), CMLL, LSE. It has a 'view at alg.cubing.net' link and a split table with columns Total/FB/SS/SP/CMLL/EOLR/EP and rows Time, Split %, STM, STPS, ETM, ETPS. Example 14020 (6.82 OH): FB 1.13s/8, SS 2.03/10, SP 0.40/4, CMLL 1.87/12, EOLR 1.39/14, 48 STM, 7.04 STPS. It also lists the other solves in the same average. Solver pages give per-method averages and F2B/L10P stage times and movecounts. Example: Crimson 3x3 Roux, 35 solves, 6.26 avg, 51.49 STM, F2B 3.14s/24.54, L10P 3.13s/26.94. OH: 25 solves, 8.31, 55.88 STM. About page: it succeeds speedcubedb, which succeeded cubesolv.es and the speedsolving Reconstruction Thread. It says it is '100% community driven, there will never be any sponsorships or ads'. FAQ: smart-cube recons were removed because of scramble randomness and because smart-cube times are not comparable. No API, licence or repository found.

resources.title: eff's Cubeast average of 100 (2H Roux, smart cube)
resources.author: eff (solver); Cubeast (platform)
resources.level: advanced (5.58 s trimmed ao100); useful as a benchmark for every level
resources.summary: A public Cubeast share page (a JS app). I rendered it with Playwright, clicked through every tab and captured the public share API responses. It records 100 smart-cube solves by eff on a MoYu AI v10 with random-state scrambles. The share is about a year old (created 2025-06-18), with about 88 views and 1 like, and commenting needs sign-in. Header: 5.58s average with the 5 best and 5 worst discarded, best 3.85, worst 10.24, 48.54 average turns, 8.604 TPS. Tabs: Average statistics, with sub-tabs Overview (stacked step bar: Pickup, Left block, Right block, CMLL, LSE, Put-down), Steps, Cases ('Case recognition is available only to Premium users'), Stats and TPS (per-step bars). Also Solves (paged table of time, turns and TPS) and Rules (standard rules: cube timer, keyboard/touch and Stackmat allowed, 3s get-ready, 15s inspection, custom scrambles off). Mean per step: Left block 0.77s execution, 7.30 turns, 9.42 TPS. Right block 0.21s recognition + 1.63s execution = 1.84s, 16.41 turns, 10.04 TPS. CMLL 0.61s recognition + 0.69s execution = 1.30s, 10.65 turns, 15.30 TPS, skipped 3%. LSE 0.37s recognition + 1.32s execution = 1.70s, 14.23 turns, 10.70 TPS. Stats: inspection 6.12s, total recognition 1.19s, total execution 4.43s. A solve's detail view shows the scramble, method (Roux), ruleset, device, a time scrubber ('0s / 3.91s', '0 / 43' moves) and step tabs (Overview, Steps, Solution, Stats, TPS). Its stored moves carry millisecond timestamps (e.g. "z'[0] y'[0] R'[0] D[84] F2[224]..."). Cubeast's Roux method definition, from the public solving_methods API, has only 4 steps: Left block, Right block, CMLL (U-adjusted, with a case set) and LSE. Each is defined as a piece-state pattern with '(LR)' axis neutrality, e.g. Left block = edges BL, FL, DL + corners DBL, DLF. There is no FS/SS/last-pair or EO/EOLR/4c split. Context: eff also wrote the open-source 'smart-roux-timer' (github.com/eff917/smart-roux-timer, GPL-3.0). It is a Xiaomi Mi smart-cube Roux timer with FB/SB/CMLL/EO/EP phase detection, built with three.js and cubing/timer; its README and LICENSE are saved.

TPS by step: SB and LSE run at about 10 TPS and CMLL at about 15 TPS. Train the blocks for fluency, not raw speed

resources.title: LaSEr v0.1 (Jade's LSE trainer)
resources.author: Jade (enbyne.tech)
resources.level: beginner to advanced (full LSE and 4c for learners; EOLR, EOLR-b and misoriented centres for advanced)
resources.summary: A static Tailwind page with 7 ES modules (lse.js, then lse/frontend, globals, cube, solver, scrambler and dict). I downloaded and read them all, then drove the trainer with Playwright. I ran the page's own code in the browser only. Model: 6 LSE edges, a centre offset and a U offset packed in a 32-bit int; moves M, M', M2, U, U', U2, or QTM-only. Practice types: Full LSE; 4a (EO relative to centres; misoriented centres accepted); EOLR (EO plus the UL/UR pieces paired in DF+DB, UF+UB or UL+UR); EOLR-b (EO plus UL/UR solved relative to the corners); and 4c (random 4c states to full solve). Settings: Only use quarter turns, Always show solution (otherwise solutions stay hidden until you solve), Max solutions (8), colour pickers for all 6 faces, Show button controls, key bindings (defaults 8=U', 9=U, 0=U2, 3=M', 2=M, 1=M2, j=reset, Enter=new), Show backside, Show bottom, Highlight UL/UR edges. EOLR settings: Allow misoriented centers in scrambles, Allow misoriented centers in solved states, Start with random AUF, and 'Possible EO states' as integer weights. Defaults are 0-0:1, Arrow:8, 1F-1B:8, 4-0:1, 0-2:1, 2LR-2:2, 2FB-0:2, 2BL-2:4, 2BL-0:4, 6-flip:1, which sum to 32 (all even-parity EO states, so the default is uniform). Settings persist in localStorage. Session: Scramble shows a case on a flat net; the scramble text is never shown. You solve with big on-screen M/M'/U/U' buttons (touch handlers) or keys. Reaching the target bolds the move line and reveals all optimal solutions with move counts. Reset replays the case. Stats: solves, your average moves, average optimum, and average efficiency (optimum/yours, %). Measured over 40 cases per mode, first-solution length: Full LSE 7-13 (mean 10.1), 4a 1-8 (4.5), EOLR 4-10 (6.8), EOLR-b 4-11 (6.9), 4c 1-7 (4.1). The shown solution solved the displayed case in 30/30 cases per mode. A U U' detour lowered efficiency to 92.9% as expected. The broken misoriented-centre setting noted on resources.rouxers.com is confirmed and root-caused. With 'Allow misoriented centers in scrambles' off, 19/60 EOLR cases still had misoriented centres (Full LSE 9/40, 4a 16/40, EOLR-b 15/40). getRandomMC itself is correct. The cause is in dict.js: loopDict stores the neighbours of the solved state with an empty move list, so every dictionary solution drops its final move ('M U' gives "U'" instead of "U' M'"). The case is built as the inverse of that truncated solution, so the real case gets an extra move. That randomly flips the centre parity, the AUF and even the EO pattern: with only 6-flip weighted, just 42/60 cases were 6-flip. The solutions shown remain correct for the case actually shown. <M,U>-optimal EOLR-b for those 6-flip cases was 9-14 STM, mostly 9-11. Same author as the enbyne.tech EOLRb trainer (deep-web-4).

resources.title: non-MU EOLRbs | cuar03
resources.author: Neo (cuar03)
resources.summary: One static HTML table (HTTP 200) using cubing.js twisty-player. Each case is drawn with an LSE-only stickering mask ('EDGES:-O-O-O-O----, CENTERS:-I-I--'), setup 'x2 y', and the alg used as the setup anchored at the end. It lists EOLRb cases whose best algs are not <M,U>-generated, which is why the rouxers hub says they are 'missing in trainers'. Purple lines are one-handed alternatives. 6-flip, with three sub-cases. (a) One LR edge on U, the other in DF: R U' r' U' M' U r U r' | r' F R U M' U' R' F' R, OH r' U r U M' U' r' U' R and (U) r U' r' U' M U r U R'. (b) One on U, the other in DB: r' F R U M' U' R' F' R (OH (U) r U' r' U' M U r U R') | R U' r' U' M' U r U r'. (c) UL/UR adjacent: r' F R U M' U' R' F' r U2 M' (OH r' U r U M' U' r' U' r U2 M') | R U' r' U' M' U r U R' U2 M'. '1/1f', UF/DB adjacent: R' F R U M' U' R' F' r (OH R' U r U M' U' r' U' r) | r U' r' U' M' U r U R'. '1/1b', UB/DF adjacent: r' F R U M U' R' F' R (OH r' U r U M U' r' U' R) | R U' r' U' M U r U r'. That is 5 cases, 10 two-handed algs and 6 OH alternatives, all variations of two skeletons: r' F R U M(') U' R' F' R/r and R U' r' U' M(') U r U r'/R'. For comparison, <M,U>-optimal EOLR-b for 6-flip cases on enbyne's laser was 9-14 STM, mostly 9-11. The 2H algs here are 9-11 moves, so the gain is ergonomics rather than movecount. The site's shared schemes.js also defines CMLL comparison stickerings (O, H, P, U1, U2, T1, T2, S1, S2, A1, A2, L1, L2 sprites), so other cuar03 sheets exist. The site root and /web/3x3/ return 404.
drills: Learn the two alg skeletons and their M/M' and r/R endings, then map each 6-flip and 1/1 sub-case onto them
Recognise 6-flip EOLRb sub-cases by where the LR edges sit (U + DF, U + DB, UL/UR adjacent)
OH: drill the purple F-less variants (r' U r U M' U' r' U' R)
infoTopics: Why some EOLRb cases are better with r/R/F moves than with <M,U>
EOLRb case naming: 6-flip, 1/1f, 1/1b, and LR edge placement
2H versus OH alg choice for LSE
